The first light of dawn barely made it through the billowing smoke. In the half-light the ruined city looked like something out of a low-budget disaster movie. Half a building still standing here and there, the windows gone. Cars burning themselves out in the middle of broad avenues. Bodies, in places several deep. The smell of burning flesh, of smoke from the fires… of a woman’s perfume…

Kostya shot upright like a released spring. Before he was properly awake he had taken cover behind the barricade of office furniture. His refuge on the top floor of an office block had no business smelling of perfume. Two mirrors, one in each corner, gave him a good view of both entrances without his having to stick his head out.

There she stood in the doorway. A lizard if ever he’d seen one. To look at, of course, she might have been any young woman who worked in an office. It was her odd manner that gave her away, the slight bend at the knees, the nervous jerk of her head. Above all it was the look in her eyes. In two months of fighting, day in, day out, Kostya had learned to spot the creatures by their eyes. One just like her had tagged along with his unit a while back. A day later she’d brought a dozen more of her kind. Relatives, she’d said. By the time anyone saw through them it was too late. Two men from the unit had lived.

Yesterday, three blocks from the office building, he’d lost the last man he had left. They’d walked into an ambush and Kostya himself had been lucky to get away. The girl’s clothes were filthy from months on the move, her hair matted. Perhaps perfume was all she had to cover the smell of an unwashed body. Or perhaps it was simply the last thing she had left of her old life.

A couple of months ago Kostya might have bought that explanation. He’d have paid for it with his life. Luckily the people at Free Will didn’t sit on information the way governments the world over did. Two months ago, two months that seemed to have gone on forever, the first warning had appeared on every television screen in the world. In two minutes a broadcast put an end to everything it had taken humanity thousands of years to build. The man on the screen introduced himself as the leader of an organization called Free Will. Its purpose, he said, was to expose an alien invasion of Earth that had so far been carried out in the utmost secrecy.

Few people took the broadcast seriously. Kostya himself had been away at a benchrest shooting match and missed it the first time around. It came to no more than a few disturbances here and there around the world among the more impressionable members of the public.

The next day Free Will went on the air again. The man whose face they now knew had fresh information from reliable sources. The invaders were a nonhumanoid race from another galaxy. Long ago they had passed to a higher plane of existence as beings of pure energy. They took possession of human bodies and fed on our consciousness, our emotions, our very life force. It was they who had given rise to the stories of evil spirits told for as long as human beings could remember. Now that Earth’s population was large enough, a mass invasion was in preparation. The governments of the world had either been bought off or were already in alien hands. Humanity’s last hope was to wake up and defend itself.

The second broadcast had considerably more effect. For two days there was rioting in every major city. People barricaded themselves in their homes and fired on anyone who came near a door or window. Self-appointed alien hunters appeared, identifying invaders by signs known only to themselves and doing their best to kill them. On the third day the authorities began to get things under control. On every television channel, on the Internet and in the press, they appealed to the public to stop the bloodshed. The Free Will broadcasts, they assured everyone, were an elaborate hoax, carefully planned and brilliantly executed.

The next broadcast undid all their efforts. Free Will reported that every government, along with its police and armed forces, had now fallen under the invaders’ influence. They were trying to regain control. The official response to the fight for liberation was proof enough. A true leader would have joined his people and led them in the fight for freedom. From this moment on, said the man on the screen, anyone connected with the government, the police or the military was automatically under suspicion.

The broadcast brought full-scale civil war to every country in the world. Soldiers who believed themselves free of infection took off their uniforms, handed out weapons to anyone willing to join them, and raised little armies of their own to fight the invasion, one another, and what was left of the regular troops. Until quite recently Kostya had belonged to one such outfit.

Free Will managed one last broadcast before the power grid collapsed and the electronic media went with it. The aliens, it warned, were adept at passing for human. They might even pose as members of the liberation movement. Watch for anything odd in their behaviour. It was against their nature to behave like human beings all the time. Sooner or later the alien’s true face would show through the human mask. Be vigilant!

Nobody ever heard from Free Will again. The war of liberation was by then in full swing. Enemy agents were exposed every day. Sometimes half an army would turn out to be the enemy and the two halves would fight to the death. Kostya himself had shot a good dozen aliens in disguise. He’d got quite handy at spotting them.

An enormous spacecraft emerged from the shadow of the Moon. Its scanners showed that the planet’s power grid was down. There was no longer any danger of detection. Taka brought the ship into orbit and silently requested his superior’s permission to speak. When it came, he took care to form the thought correctly.

The population is down to one tenth of its former numbers. The power grid has been destroyed. The use of the most powerful weapons has left two thirds of the planet uninhabitable for the natives. One full orbit of the star from now, the planet will be ready for settlement without recourse to military force.

At the far end of the chamber Thorg sat comfortably back on his tail. He could read Taka’s thoughts as easily as he could frame his own. There was a reason his name was one symbol longer. The junior’s efforts amused him, and there were splendid prospects in the discovery he had made. How a rather dim subordinate of his had hit on such a remarkable idea was more than Thorg could fathom. In one claw he was turning a small cylindrical object used for storing information, a sik. Encoded in the DNA of a specially bred bacterium inside it was the junior’s treatise on the conquest of industrialized worlds.

The Council of Aggressors would be delighted. They could now conquer advanced industrial worlds at practically no expense. For the past few millennia the Council had been cutting military spending and confining its conquests to underdeveloped planets. Technological civilizations, in the Council’s opinion, cost too much to conquer. And along comes silly little Taka with his trick for starting trouble through a planet’s own information network. Research showed that every technologically advanced civilization had one.

A little research, a carefully contrived provocation, and the natives went to war with one another. Minimal outlay, no casualties, and the planet was theirs. He, Thorg, conqueror of worlds, would have a seat on the Council of Aggressors. He might even come to preside over it. As for the death of an insignificant junior called Taka, who would notice?

Taka held himself motionless in an attitude of respect, awaiting a reply. He was a good deal less stupid than his superior supposed and had long since guessed what thoughts were going round in Thorg’s vain head. This discovery was to have been Taka’s way up. It might be worth three new symbols to his name at a stroke. Takargh. That had a fine sound to it. A chief’s name, a far cry from that of a miserable junior aboard a scout ship. And now that he had conquered an industrial world with one all but unarmed ship and a crew of two scouts, his dream had never been closer.
His superior’s attention came back to him. Good work, Taka. The Council will hear of your discovery. You will be rewarded.
Taka took the opportunity to put his suspicions to the test. May I enter some new data on the sik? He bowed, his whole bearing an expression of submission.
His superior stiffened. The junior’s uneasiness had not escaped him. After a moment Thorg made up his mind. You can do that later. I want to go over the research once more.

Taka bowed again and turned to the console. That settled it. Thorg had no intention of letting the research out of his claws. The junior reached for the ray gun in its recess in the console. A blinding flash. He seized the gun and fired without aiming. In the same instant something struck him a tremendous blow in the chest.

Thorg was sliding slowly out of his chair. His arm and part of his torso had vanished, along with the sik that held the research findings. Taka lay slumped across the console, shot clean through the chest. Thorg put aside his annoyance at the loss of the data, fell to the deck and, with what strength he had left, began to crawl towards the console.

The enormous disc-shaped ship turned in orbit around the war-torn planet. So many explosions had turned the atmosphere grey, streaked with brown. Neither oceans nor continents could be seen. Nuclear winter was setting in. The last days allotted to humanity were drawing to a close.

A claw caught the edge of the console. Trembling fingers reached for the emergency panel, leaving brown streaks on the grey metal. The shrill note of a distress alarm filled the chamber. The claw slipped from the console. A heavy body hit the deck.

The Council of Aggressors had never been in such a state. Every member had at least ten symbols to his name, and their mastery of telepathy was of the highest order, yet any telepath who set foot in the council chamber just then risked losing his mind. Thoughts darted from one councillor to the next, tangled, joined to form collective images, warped, and sometimes, under the pressure of the mental fields in the room, spontaneously turned into their opposites. At last the Chairman of the Council of Aggressors put an end to the disorder with a request sharp enough, and insistent enough, to compel attention.

“The problem before us is a new one. We do not yet know how to combat the invader our rescue crews brought back to our world when they towed the damaged scout ship home. Most of what we know comes from a translation of a recording in which one of the natives of the planet destroyed by the invaders can be seen speaking. Evidently our scouts were attempting to investigate events on the occupied planet. In the course of that investigation the junior, whose name was Taka, was infected by an invading organism and attacked his superior, Thorg. Although mortally wounded in repelling the attack, the senior scout managed to send us a distress signal. Regrettably, we did not immediately understand his warning.

“We know from the translation that these organisms take possession of individual natives and in this way gradually gain control over an entire civilization. The first signs of an invasion are already apparent. Each day brings more reports of strange behaviour among the inhabitants of our worlds. We have also received word that citizens are forming militias to hunt down the invaders and are circulating the alien recording in translation. For the first time in our history it is we who have been subjected to aggression. Hitherto it has been our privilege to do the conquering. We must be vigilant. We know from the recording that the first to be infected are members of the government and the military.”
A tense silence fell. The members of the Council of Aggressors eyed one another suspiciously, as though they had never met.

The girl had heard something rustle, or perhaps she’d heard Kostya breathing. He couldn’t wait any longer. In one movement he came up on one knee. Two sharp cracks. The smell of gunpowder. Kostya stepped over the body and out onto the stairs. The air in the street was stale, though fresher than it had been on the top floor. Things weren’t so bad. Two months since the world had gone off the rails and here he was, still alive. There was an answer for his wife the next time she asked what good that stupid shooting of his would ever do him.

Snow began to fall in great flakes. There was definitely something wrong with the world. It was the middle of July. Still, life went on. He had to find his own people and fight the enemy. Kostya pulled his thin windbreaker tight around him and set off towards the sound of distant gunfire.
